summary: A glossary of terminology used in routing requirements and solutions for Low-Power and Lossy Networks, composed of many resource-limited embedded devices. It helps keep terminology consistent across related documents.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7102 is a word list. It fixes the names used for the parts of a network made of tiny battery-powered devices, so that an industrial monitoring document and a smart home document talk about the same sensor, the same border router and the same direction of travel. Later routing specifications for these networks are expected to use these words.

subtitle: The shared vocabulary for routing in networks of tiny, battery-powered devices.

tldr.problem: Networks of sensors and actuators are built for wildly different industries, and each industry tends to invent its own name for the same device, so documents about routing them use different words for the same thing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC fixes a common set of terms for the routing working group to use, covering the devices, the network shape, the direction of traffic and the way the devices sleep and wake.
tldr.outcome: The document is a glossary, not a protocol. It defines no procedures and raises no security issues of its own, and it is expected that later routing documents will cite it.

facts.label: Typical data rates
facts.value: A few kilobits to a few hundred kilobits per second

facts.label: Routing protocol
facts.value: RPL, an IPv6 routing protocol for LLNs

today: RFC 7102 is an Informational RFC published in January 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a glossary of terms for the routing working group, intended to be cited as an informative reference by later documents rather than to be implemented.

sections.title: Why a Shared Word List
sections.content:
The document provides a glossary of the terminology used in routing requirements and solutions for networks referred to as Low-Power and Lossy Networks. Such a network is typically composed of many embedded devices with limited power, memory and processing resources, interconnected by a variety of links such as IEEE 802.15.4 or low-power Wi-Fi.

There is a wide scope of application areas, including industrial monitoring, building automation for heating, ventilation, air conditioning, lighting, access control and fire, connected home, health care, environmental monitoring, urban sensor networks, energy management, assets tracking, and refrigeration. Since these applications are usually highly specific, it is not uncommon to see a number of disparate terms used to describe the same device or functionality. To avoid confusion or discrepancies, the document specifies the common terminology to be used in all the documents of the routing working group, and the terms it defines are already used in the routing requirement documents for urban, industrial, home and building networks.

Terminology specific to a particular application is out of scope. The expectation is that all routing documents defining requirements or specifying solutions for these networks will use the common terminology, and that this document should be listed as an informative reference.
sections.plainLanguage: Every industry calls the same little box a different name. Once you are writing about how such devices route their messages, you need one set of names, and this RFC is that set.

sections.title: The Devices and the Network
sections.content:
A field device is a physical device placed in the network's operating environment, such as a plant, an urban area or a home. Field devices include sensors and actuators as well as routers and border routers, and are usually, though not always, constrained in processor, memory footprint, storage capacity, bandwidth and sometimes power. For illustration, a typical sensor or actuator would have a few kilobytes of RAM, a few dozens of kilobytes of read-only or flash memory, an 8-, 16- or 32-bit microcontroller, and communication capabilities ranging from a few kilobits per second to a few hundred kilobits per second. Even as hardware improves, such devices are likely to keep looking resource-constrained next to the computers and routers used in the rest of the internet.

A sensor measures a physical quantity and converts it into an analogue or digital signal that can be read by a program or a person, of many kinds: electromagnetic, such as current, voltage, power or resistance, mechanical, such as pressure, flow, liquid density or humidity, chemical, such as oxygen or carbon monoxide, and acoustic, such as noise or ultrasound. An actuator is a field device that controls a set of equipment, for example modulating the flow of a gas or liquid, controlling electricity distribution, or performing a mechanical operation. A controller is a field device that can receive sensor input and automatically change the environment in the facility by manipulating digital or analogue actuators. A data sink is a device that collects data from nodes in the network.

The border router of a low-power and lossy network connects that network to another routing domain, such as a local area network, a wide area network or the internet, where a different routing protocol may be in operation. It acts as a routing device and may also host other functions such as a data collector or aggregator. The routing structure itself is a directed acyclic graph: a collection of vertices and directed edges where each edge connects one vertex to another, such that there is no way to start at some vertex and follow a sequence of edges that eventually loops back to where you started. RPL is the IPv6 routing protocol for these networks. It supports multipoint-to-point traffic from devices inside the network towards a central control point, point-to-multipoint traffic from that control point back out to the devices, and point-to-point traffic between any two nodes. An RPL domain is a collection of RPL routers under the control of a single administration, with the boundaries of routing domains set by network management marking some links as exterior or inter-domain links.
sections.plainLanguage: The vocabulary covers the sensors that read the world, the actuators that change it, the controllers that connect the two, the little routers in between, and the border router that joins the whole thing to the internet.

sections.title: Direction, Traffic Patterns and Sleeping Devices
sections.content:
Direction is defined relative to the network. Upstream is the data direction travelling from inside the network out through the border router to a local area network, a wide area network or the internet, or generally closer to the root of the directed acyclic graph computed by the routing protocol. Downstream is the opposite: data travelling from outside the network in through the border router, or generally deeper into the graph.

Three traffic patterns are named. Point to point is traffic exchanged between two nodes, whatever the number of hops between them. Point-to-multipoint is traffic between one node and a set of nodes, a concept much like the one used in multicast or in MPLS traffic engineering; a common use of RPL involves point-to-multipoint flows from or through the root of the graph outwards towards the other nodes. Multipoint-to-point describes a traffic pattern such as flows collecting information from many nodes and flowing upstream towards a collecting sink or a border router.

Because the devices have so little power, they sleep. A sleepy node may sometimes go into a sleep mode, a low-power state that conserves power, and temporarily suspend protocol communication; when it is not asleep it is fully powered on and able to communicate. A non-sleepy node is always fully powered on and always able to communicate. Around this sit the radio terms. A channel is a radio frequency sub-band used to transmit a modulated signal carrying packets, and channel hopping is the procedure by which field devices synchronously change channels while operating. A timeslot is a fixed time interval that may be used for the transmission or reception of a packet between two field devices, and a timeslot used for communications is associated with a slotted link. A schedule is an agreed execution, wake-up, transmission or reception timetable between two or more field devices. The packet error rate is the ratio of the number of unusable packets, whether not received at all or received in error after any applicable error correction, to the total number that would have been received without errors.
sections.plainLanguage: The same terms are used for which way data is going and for how the radios share the air. Nodes spend most of their time asleep, so the routing has to work with devices that are only occasionally listening.

sections.title: The Vocabulary of Particular Industries
sections.content:
Several terms belong to the application areas rather than to routing. Advanced metering infrastructure uses smart grid technologies, and a canonical smart grid application is smart metering. Distribution automation is part of the smart grid and encompasses technologies for the maintenance and management of electrical distribution systems. A smart grid is a broad class of applications that network and automate utility infrastructure. The facility management system is a global term applied across all the vertical designations within a building, including heating, ventilation and air conditioning, fire, security, lighting and elevator control. The Highway Addressable Remote Transducer group of specifications covers industrial process and control devices, and its latest version, HART7, includes the additions for WirelessHART. The International Society of Automation is an accredited standards-making society, and ISA100 is one of its committees, whose charter includes defining a family of standards for industrial automation, with a working group inside it working on a standard for monitoring and non-critical process-control applications.

Two control models are distinguished. Under closed loop control, a device controller controls an actuator based on input information sensed by one or more field devices. Under open loop control, a plant operator manually manipulates an actuator over the network, with the decision influenced by information sensed by field devices. A commissioning tool is any physical or logical device temporarily added to the network for the express purpose of setting up the network and the device operational parameters, and it can also be added temporarily for scheduled or unscheduled maintenance. The document also names radio frequency identification, the medium access control algorithms used by the data link layer to coordinate use of the physical layer, and the memory types the devices use: RAM is volatile, ROM is read-only, and flash memory is non-volatile but can be re-programmed.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of the words belong to a particular industry: what a smart meter is called, what a plant operator does differently from a controller, and what a maintenance laptop is called when it is plugged in for an afternoon.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The RFC is one paragraph long on security. Since the document specifies terminology and does not specify new procedures or protocols, it raises no new security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: A word list cannot introduce a security problem, because it introduces no behaviour. The document says exactly that and stops there.

viz.caption: THE CORE VOCABULARY OF THE GLOSSARY

items.title: Field device
items.text: A physical device in the operating environment, usually with very little memory, processor and power.

items.title: Sensor
items.text: Measures a physical quantity and turns it into a signal a program can read.

items.title: Actuator
items.text: Controls equipment, such as the flow of a gas or an electric supply.

items.title: Controller
items.text: Takes sensor input and changes the environment by driving actuators.

items.title: Border router
items.text: Connects the network to another routing domain, and may collect data as well.

items.title: Data sink
items.text: The device that collects data from the nodes in the network.

viz.caption: UPSTREAM AND DOWNSTREAM, AS DEFINED IN RFC 7102

left.title: Upstream
left.desc: Data travelling out of the network, and generally closer to the root of the routing graph.

right.title: Downstream
right.desc: Data travelling into the network from outside, and generally deeper into the routing graph.
